title: Learning to Classify Threading in Melts of Rings
authors: Filippo Conforto, Roman Staňo, Jan Smrek, Davide Michieletto
abstract: Dense melts of nonconcatenated ring polymers exhibit anomalous dynamics and nonlinear rheology, in some cases linked to long-lived inter-ring threading entanglement. Detecting these geometric constraints remains computationally demanding, with different methods being based on different geometric features tuned to specific models. Here, we introduce a machine-learning framework that detects threading directly from the writhe of ring conformations and we demonstrate its broad generalisability. Trained on simulations of isolated, distance-constrained pairs of short rings, a one-dimensional convolutional neural network (CNN1D) operating on the writhe profile classifies threading states with over 98% accuracy on held-out ring pairs. Remarkably, this model generalises without retraining to equilibrium dense melts spanning a wide range of densities and chain lengths (N = 100 to 1600), maintaining true-positive rates above 91% with false-positive rates near zero. Misclassified conformations are limited to physically ambiguous, shallow threading events which are arguably not impacting the dynamics of the rings. Effectively, writhe captures the interaction between the two rings, allowing writhe-based classifiers to improve the topological analysis of large ring-polymer systems with a 3-fold speed-up over the state-of-the-art minimal-surface detection. These results establish the writhe-trained neural networks as an accurate, scalable tool for characterising entanglement in ring polymer melts.
summary: This work introduces a novel, scalable machine-learning approach to characterize topological entanglement (threading) in dense polymer melts. By training a 1D CNN on the writhe profile, the authors developed a method that accurately and rapidly classifies these complex interactions, significantly improving upon existing computationally intensive topological analysis techniques.
main_problem: The paper addresses the computationally demanding task of detecting and classifying inter-ring threading entanglement in dense melts of nonconcatenated ring polymers.
main_result: A CNN1D trained on the writhe profile achieves high accuracy (>98%) and generalizes robustly to dense melts, offering a 3-fold speed-up over state-of-the-art minimal-surface detection methods.
method: A machine-learning framework utilizing a one-dimensional Convolutional Neural Network (CNN1D) is employed to classify threading states directly from the calculated writhe profile of ring conformations.
model_or_system: The physical system is a dense melt of nonconcatenated ring polymers simulated using a coarse-grained bead-spring model with WCA and FENE potentials. The analysis focuses on topological constraints like inter-ring threading.
key_observables: Threading status (binary classification), writhe profile/density, separation length ($L_{sep}$), and classification accuracy/F1 score.
important_parameters: Chain lengths ($N=100$ to $1600$), melt densities ($ho$), and the writhe profile itself.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the writhe captures the essential local interaction information required for topological classification, allowing the ML model to generalize from dilute training sets to dense melts.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate representative configurations of threaded/non-threaded rings using minimal surfaces, compare the performance of CNN2D vs. CNN1D on writhe features, and demonstrate the model's generalization across varying densities and chain lengths.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem, details the feature engineering (writhe profile calculation), compares ML architectures (RNN, CNN2D, CNN1D), presents results showing CNN1D's superior performance and generalization, and concludes with the computational and physical advantages of the writhe-based approach.
why_interesting: While the system is classical polymer physics, the core methodology—using deep learning (CNNs) on derived geometric features (writhe) to solve a complex topological classification problem—is highly relevant to ML-physics applications in condensed matter.
